article_title: Sound Partners
citation: Sound Partners. (2010). WWC Intervention Report: Sound Partners. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. http://www.wri-edu.org/partners/sound-partners.htm
title: Short frequent one-to-one tutoring sessions with scripted phonics lessons and mastery checks
description: The program's instructional pattern is "30 minute sessions of one-to-one tutoring that take place four days per week throughout one school year." Reading fluency and accuracy

description: Lally's 'social womb' framework holds that, for the first few years of life, the brain needs "a safe, nurturing, and stimulating environment in which babies can learn how to interact with others and use the tools of society to get their needs met." citation: Darling-Hammond, L., Flook, L., Schachner, A., & Wojcikiewicz, S. (with Cantor, P., & Osher, D.). (2021). Educator learning to enact the science of learning and development. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/859.776

citation: Fitz, J. (with Price, H.). (2025). Positive conditions for mathematics learning: An overview of the research. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/967.472
title: Science of learning and development (SoLD) framework: students learn best in environments offering safety, positive relationships, belonging, purpose, and affirmation
description: The report organizes its synthesis around the science of learning and development (SoLD), a body of research from neuroscience, psychology, and developmental and learning sciences. title: Social network analysis framework of nodes, ties, and social capital for understanding educational reform sustainability
description: The report applies social network theory to statewide reform: a social network is "a group of actors connected to one another through a set of relations or ties." Nodes are the actors (people, groups, organizations); ties are the connections or flows between them, which link up to form paths allowing nodes to directly or indirectly influence one another. Strong ties support transfer of tacit, non-routine and complex knowledge, while weaker, less dense networks suit simple routine information. Social capital is "an investment in a system's social relations through which the resources of other individuals can be accessed, borrowed, or leveraged." The report uses this framework to analyze how AD networks spread the initiative and may sustain it.
requirements: Mapping of both formal and informal structures, since informal ties can impact the success of formal structures
constraints: The report notes it did not find examples fitting the transforming level of interaction, so that level was not used in its analysis

article_title: 'It Felt a Bit Eerie": Exploring Humanlike Interactions During Collaborative Writing with an Artificial Agent'
citation: Michael Yin, Angela Chiang, Samuel Rhys Cox, and Robert Xiao. (2026). "It Felt a Bit Eerie": Exploring Humanlike Interactions During Collaborative Writing with an Artificial Agent. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24729
title: Social presence with social costs: humanlike interaction design of artificial agents
description: An account extending CASA theory to interaction-level design cues: shaping when (temporal humanlikeness) and how (visual humanlikeness) an agent interacts elicits social presence, which supports collaboration (efficiency, intent understanding, social connection) but also produces social costs such as feeling watched, judged, distracted, and misaligned. As the authors put it, "while humanlike collaborative systems do elicit social presence, this can potentially lead to social costs as well". The account holds that these costs are exacerbated without the alignment present in human–human collaboration, and can be somewhat alleviated through visible alignment and shared understanding.
requirements: Interaction design cues (synchrony, apparent effort via cursor) that participants read as humanlike
constraints: Studied in a collaborative writing task with an LLM peer editor; costs arise especially without human–human-style alignment
target_learners: adult writers collaborating with AI agents
target_learning_goals: effective and socially comfortable human–AI collaborative writing
examples: The three-variant user study manipulated temporal and visual humanlikeness and traced both benefits (efficiency, understanding) and costs (surveillance, overload) to social presence

citation: Yilmaz A (2026) The psychological mechanisms and behavioral determinants of academic integrity in the age of artificial intelligence. Front. Psychol. 17:1853790. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1853790
title: Stimulus–Organism–Response framework for AI-assisted academic dishonesty as a moderated mediation process
description: The article organizes AI-assisted academic dishonesty within the Stimulus–Organism–Response (SOR) framework, in which psychological vulnerabilities and socio-contextual conditions act as stimuli, cheating tendency is the organismic mechanism, and dishonesty is the behavioral response, with AI use as a moderating technological condition. The authors state the "SOR framework is well aligned with the proposed moderated mediation model, as it explains how psychological and contextual stimuli may be linked to AI-assisted academic dishonesty through cheating tendency." The model was tested with 1,045 undergraduates using PROCESS Model 14.
requirements: Measurement of psychological antecedents, cheating tendency, AI use, dishonesty, and social-contextual factors as distinct constructs
constraints: AI use is positioned as a behavioral amplifier in a non-causal statistical sense, not a direct cause of unethical behavior
target_learning_goals: academic integrity
ethical use of AI in academic work
examples: The study tested the model with seven measurement instruments, Pearson correlations, multiple regression, and Hayes' PROCESS Model 14 with 5,000-sample bootstrapping.

description: The paper's explanatory framework is that emerging human-AI collaboration skills are best learned through adaptive, interactive, context-aware guidance embedded in the learner's workflow rather than static formats. citation: Cassandra Lucas, Anshul Bihani, Rohini Kukka, Chun-Hua Tsai, Jaydeb Sarker, and Mia Mohammad Imran. 2026. TowardsSocratiCode: Designing a Generative AI-Based Programming Tutor for K-12 Students through a 4-Week Participatory Design Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17857
title: SocratiCode: a Socratic, adaptive generative-AI tutoring framework for beginner programming
description: SocratiCode is a prompt-based generative-AI tutoring framework that operationalizes Socratic tutoring principles—guided questioning, reflection, incremental hints, and learner-paced progression—for K-12 beginner programming. It embeds structural elements such as introductions, examples, practice, summaries, and follow-up tasks that "maintain coherence and create natural stopping points," and elicits minimal background information to adjust pacing, analogies, and explanations. The framework draws on adaptive learning theory, generative-AI education research, prompt engineering, and Socratic tutoring principles, and was refined through participatory design with two K-12 learners.

Structural prompt components (role, lesson flow, checkpoints, closure, interaction rules, scope constraints) to maintain coherence and stopping points

Findings are preliminary; other generative AI models may behave differently under similar conditions
target_learners: K-12 novice programmers with no prior programming experience
target_learning_goals: Introductory Python programming concepts and problem-solving skills
examples: The final prompt template specified role and audience, learner adaptation, lesson flow, reinforcement, tutorial closure with a hard-stop, interaction rules pausing after exercises, and scope constraints teaching only requested concepts

citation: Ilya Mikhelson. (2026). The Theoretical Foundation of Socratic Tests: Dynamic, Multimodal, Conversational Examinations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29624
title: The Socratic Test framework: decoupled Bloom's prompting and SOLO evaluation to map the Zone of Proximal Development
description: The Socratic Test is an adaptive, typed conversational assessment that standardizes the method of measurement without standardizing prompts. It decouples two taxonomies: "Bloom's Taxonomy dictates the cognitive difficulty of theprompt, the AI utilizes the SOLO Taxonomy... to measure the structural quality of theresponse." Rooted in Dynamic Assessment, it quantifies the ZPD by differentiating Independent from Assisted Performance via a scaffolding discount factor. SOLO's structural criteria are presented as observable and defensible, shifting grading from semantic interpretation to structural complexity.

constraints: Real-time SOLO assessment is strictly provisional and conservative; inaccuracies are absorbed by the oversampled evidence buffer and corrected in the post-exam pipeline

citation: Ilya Mikhelson. (2026). The Theoretical Foundation of Socratic Tests: Dynamic, Multimodal, Conversational Examinations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29624
title: socratictest.com: a summative conversational assessment platform with evidence buffers, shadow ledger, and human-AI grading pipeline
description: The author developed socratictest.com, "a custom software platform explicitly engineered to administer the Socratic Test modality," architected as a summative assessment engine with a decoupled design separating the real-time proctoring engine from the final deterministic gradebook. Core mechanics include an oversampled Evidence Buffer (e.g., 120%), a hidden Shadow Ledger logging baseline point values for skipped or exhausted prompts, user-directed pivoting with state resurrection, an Out-of-Scope audit protocol, and a 7-step grading pipeline with instructor calibration, validation, override, and an appeals queue.

description: The study grounds its design in Vygotsky's social constructivism, in which "These interactions serve as cognitive scaffolding, supporting less proficient learners in the acquisition and development of their knowledge". Soft forms — hedging, yes-but partial agreement, posing an alternative idea, indirect challenge, and prosody — "were used to imply disagreements rather than overtly contradict others' ideas." title: Social reasoning as a multi-perspective social-cognitive capacity for justifying social decisions
description: The article defines social reasoning as "a social-cognitive capacity to consider, interpret and weigh upon multiple aspects of a complex social situation... in order to make informed social decisions." It is treated as one of the most difficult forms of reasoning because social situations contain information that is biased, fragmented, and uncertain. Reasoning about a social-moral issue requires coordinating three theory-driven perspectives — moral (obligatory virtues such as fairness and honesty), societal (authority, traditions, norms), and personal-relational (individual needs, emotions, motivations) — and justifying knowledge with reasons or evidence meeting logical integrity, clarity, credibility, and accessibility.

justification of social knowledge with reasons and evidence

article_title: Assumptions and confidence of others: the impact of socio-cognitive information on metacognitive self-regulation
citation: Schnaubert, L., Krukowski, S., & Bodemer, D. (2021). Assumptions and confidence of others: the impact of socio-cognitive information on metacognitive self-regulation. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09269-5
title: Socio-cognitive information as an external cue in metacognitive monitoring and control
description: The article frames other people's assumptions and confidence as external cues that learners may consult when forming metacognitive judgments, extending cue-based accounts of confidence judgments beyond internally generated information. It states that "the assumptions of other individuals might be used as an external cue validating or contradicting own initial assumptions, especially in the case of limited information requiring inductive inference". Within the Nelson-and-Narens monitoring/control cycle, such cues adjust confidence on the meta-level, which then steers control decisions such as information search. The empirical study tests this account by confronting learners with a partner's answers and confidence.
requirements: Learners must perceive socio-cognitive information such as another person's assumptions and stated confidence in the learning environment.
constraints: The studied scenario was minimalistic: an unknown, computer-generated partner with no further social cues or instructions on how to use the information.
target_learners: university students in self-regulated learning settings, especially online learning environments
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring and control of learning, including confidence judgments and study decisions such as information search
examples: Participants read expository texts, judged true-false statements on a combined confidence/answer scale, viewed a computer-generated partner's answers and confidence, then re-judged and could request additional information.

article_title: Co-regulation of learning in computer-supported collaborative learning environments: a discussion
citation: Carol K. K. Chan. (2012). Co-regulation of learning in computer-supported collaborative learning environments: a discussion. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 63–73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-012-9086-z
title: Social metacognition and collective regulation account of co-regulated learning in CSCL
description: The review advances a socio-cognitive account in which regulation in collaborative learning extends self-regulation to social and collective levels. It argues that "working in groups may help students develop social metacognition and become more aware of what they do not understand", and that students must develop metacognitive awareness of their team's state of knowledge, since only when students perceive gaps in the group's knowledge do they exert regulatory strategies. It extends this to collective regulation, with students focusing on the group-team as a collective entity, moving from 'I' to 'We' perspectives.
requirements: Models of co-regulation need to include elements of metacognitive knowledge
constraints: The review notes much controversy and confusion about the regulation and metacognition constructs, and that current analyses emphasize frequencies of strategies rather than quality and depth of conceptual processing
target_learning_goals: co-regulation, social metacognition, awareness of own and group knowledge gaps

article_title: Metacognitive awareness as measured by second-order judgements among university and secondary school students
citation: Marloes L. Nederhand, Huib K. Tabbers, Anique B.H. De Bruin, Remy M. J. P. Rikers. (2021). Metacognitive awareness as measured by second-order judgements among university and secondary school students. Metacognition and Learning, 16, 1-14. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09228-6
title: Second-order judgements as a measure of metacognitive awareness that hinges on calibration accuracy rather than performance level
description: The article frames metacognitive awareness in calibration research as having two components: functional confidence (the performance estimate itself) and subjective confidence (the confidence assigned to that estimate), the latter measured by a second-order judgement (SOJ). On this account, students are metacognitively aware when their SOJs align with their calibration accuracy, "irrespective of students' performance level". The study's university results support the alignment account, while the secondary school results mark a developmental boundary.
requirements: Students must provide both a performance estimate and a confidence rating of that estimate (SOJ) so alignment between subjective confidence and calibration accuracy can be examined
constraints: The alignment between SOJs and calibration accuracy was found for university students but not for secondary school students, suggesting the account applies only once metacognitive awareness is more developed
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of exam performance
metacognitive monitoring of calibration accuracy
examples: After taking their exams, students estimated their grade on a 10-point scale and rated confidence in the estimate on a five-point scale, allowing the alignment of SOJs with absolute difference scores of calibration to be tested.

article_title: Examining the regulation of motivational and comprehension-related problems during collaborative learning
citation: Nadine Melzner · Markus Dresel · Ingo Kollar. (2022). Examining the regulation of motivational and comprehension-related problems during collaborative learning. Metacognition and Learning (2022) 17:813–836. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09316-9
title: Three social levels of regulation in collaborative learning (self, co, shared)
description: The article adopts Järvelä and Hadwin's (2013) distinction of three social levels at which groups can regulate learning. At the self-level strategies are applied "without making them visible for the other group members"; at the co-level "a student may try to support single fellow group members to improve their learning processes"; at the shared-level groups "share, negotiate, and synthetize strategies to attain joint learning goals", which the article terms an instance of shared regulation. The same strategy can operate at each level, e.g. self-explaining terms, asking one member to explain, or jointly developing shared understanding.
requirements: Groups whose members can distinguish which regulation activities are directed at their own learning, at other individual members' learning, or at the group's joint learning
constraints: Research based on this three-level model is described in the article as having a strong qualitative focus, and empirical evidence on which problems get regulated at which level was scarce
target_learners: university students in self-formed study groups
target_learning_goals: regulating motivational and comprehension-related problems during collaborative exam preparation
examples: Participants rated and described strategies at each level after every vignette; the soccer example vignette illustrated level distinctions such as 'We eat pizza together to strengthen our team spirit' as a shared-level motivational strategy

citation: Nadira Saab. (2012). Team regulation, regulation of social activities or co-regulation: Different labels for effective regulation of learning in CSCL. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9085-5
title: Levels of social interaction framework for regulative activities in CSCL: individual, dyadic, and group levels
description: The article organizes regulative activities during collaborative learning by the social level at which they occur. It states that "During collaborative learning, the regulation of activities can take place at different levels of social interaction: the individual level, the dyadic level, and the group level." Individual regulation is an intrapersonal process regulating one's own cognitive processes; dyadic regulation means one member regulates another member's activities; group-level regulation involves shared activities aimed at regulating the group's cognitive activities. Dyadic and group regulation are characterized as interpersonal processes. The article uses this framework to map the three special-issue studies (Fig. 1).
requirements: Regulative activities must be coded or observed in a collaborative setting so the social level at which they occur can be distinguished
constraints: The article notes the Meijer et al. coding scheme used by Lajoie and Lu was developed for individuals working alone and "it is not possible to code regulative activities at a dyadic level" with it

examples: Fig. 1 maps Saab et al.'s task and team regulation, Janssen et al.'s task-related and social regulation, and Lajoie and Lu's metacognitive activities and co-regulation onto the three levels

article_title: What Does Research Say About the Science of Reading for K-5 Multilingual Learners? A Systematic Review of Systematic Reviews
citation: Kittle, J. M., Amendum, S. J., & Budde, C. M. (2024). What Does Research Say About the Science of Reading for K-5 Multilingual Learners? A Systematic Review of Systematic Reviews. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09942-6
title: Four-cluster evidence-based component model of the science of reading for K-5 multilingual learners
description: This review of reviews organizes the science of reading for K-5 multilingual learners into four broad clusters of components related to English reading comprehension: "oral language, phonological awareness (PA), decoding and oral reading fluency, and reading comprehension." Each cluster includes components in both MLs' first language and English, and the review grounds the framework in the Simple View of Reading (RC = D × LC) and Scarborough's Reading Rope, extended by multilingual theories such as Bernhardt's compensatory model in which knowledge sources interact synergistically, not additively.
requirements: Components must be directly related to English reading comprehension outcomes, in accordance with the SVR, as the review's inclusion criterion required
constraints: The review notes reading comprehension is widely considered multidimensional rather than a unitary construct and is likely less componential
Evidence is drawn from reviews of studies conducted primarily in U.S. K-5 classrooms, with at least 50% of studies in that setting

article_title: Interactivity in Video-based Models
citation: Wouters, P., Tabbers, H. K., & Paas, F. (2007). Interactivity in Video-based Models. Educational Psychology Review, 19, 327–342. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9045-4
title: Social cognitive model of sequential skill acquisition
description: This model describes how learners move from observing a model to independent, self-regulated performance. As the review states, "The model contends that skills can be optimally acquired in four sequential stages": observation, emulation or imitation, self-control, and self-regulation. The review uses it as the organizing framework, arguing that the transition from observing to self-regulated practice is accompanied by different cognitive processes and different forms of interactivity, and that both delayed and premature starts with actual performance can hamper learning.
requirements: Learners must transition from observation to performance in a timely way; both delayed and premature transitions can hamper learning
constraints: Initially learners depend heavily on the performance and standards of the model and must gradually rely more on their own self-regulation processes
target_learners: novices learning complex motor or cognitive skills
target_learning_goals: acquisition of complex skills through observation leading to self-regulated performance
examples: The review maps each interactivity guideline to one or more of the four stages, e.g., pacing in the observation stage and reflection prompts in the self-control and self-regulation stages

article_title: Social Presence: Conceptualization and Measurement
citation: Karel Kreijns, Kate Xu, Joshua Weidlich. (2022). Social Presence: Conceptualization and Measurement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09623-8
title: Reformulated definition of social presence as perceived 'realness' of other persons in technology-mediated communication
description: The review reformulates Short et al.'s (1976) definition of social presence, which it finds ambiguous and non-operationalizable because 'salience' admits multiple interpretations. The reformulated definition treats social presence as 'the psychological phenomenon in which, to a certain extent, the others are perceived as physical "real" persons in technology-mediated communication enabled by CMC tools and electronic platforms'. It is a sense of others being present in the here and now even when they are not — 'the illusion of being together with other persons as if the communication is not mediated at all'. This makes 'realness' the underlying latent construct that can be assessed.
requirements: The construct must be operationalized by assessing perceived 'realness' of the other persons, not attitudes toward the communication medium
constraints: The article states the reformulated definition departs from Short et al.'s technological determinism, so realness is not determined solely by medium attributes
target_learners: online distance education learners in group learning settings
target_learning_goals: interpersonal communication and group dynamics in online group learning
examples: The authors ground the reformulation in Short et al.'s own statements that social presence depends on the degree to which the other person is perceived as a 'real' person, including their expectation of three-dimensional electronic reconstitution of distant individuals

article_title: Social Presence: Conceptualization and Measurement
citation: Karel Kreijns, Kate Xu, Joshua Weidlich. (2022). Social Presence: Conceptualization and Measurement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09623-8
title: Triangle model interrelating social presence, sociability, and social space with social interaction at the center
description: The review identifies two constructs closely linked to social presence: sociability, defined as 'the capacity of CMC tools and electronic platforms to allow for the expression of social presence and the experience of it as well as for the emergence of a social space', a medium attribute; and social space, 'the network of interpersonal relationships embedded in group structures of norms and values, rules and roles, and beliefs and ideals', a group attribute manifested by sense of community, group climate, mutual trust, social identity, and group cohesion. The three constructs are shown as a triangle whose sides represent their interrelations, with social interaction at the center, since together they influence how social interaction in groups is established and maintained.
requirements: The three constructs must be treated as interrelated rather than in isolation, because together they influence how social interaction in groups is established and maintained
constraints: The article states most social presence researchers, unaware of sociability and social space, collapse the three constructs into one 'social presence' construct
target_learners: learners in online group learning and learning networks
target_learning_goals: establishing and maintaining social interaction in online groups
examples: Figure 1 visually depicts the triangle with social presence, sociability, and social space as vertices and social interaction positioned in the center

article_title: The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development
citation: Sarit Barzilai & Clark A. Chinn. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09927-5
title: Sosa's reliabilist virtue epistemology grounds the Apt-AIR goal of fully apt epistemic performance through success, competence, and aptness conditions
description: The Apt-AIR framework is grounded in the reliabilist virtue epistemology of philosopher Ernest Sosa. Sosa proposed that an epistemic performance can be evaluated by examining three conditions: its success in attaining its aim, whether it is an exercise of competence using appropriate strategies, and whether it is apt, meaning successful because it is competent. Real achievement requires not just success but apt success, because competent performance reduces the risk of failure. Performance guided by meta-level awareness of one's competence is described as fully apt performance. The article states that "the aim of epistemic education should be to promote learners' fully apt epistemic performance."
requirements: Educators adopting this goal must consider not only whether learners succeed but whether success derives from reliable processes rather than guessing or luck
constraints: What counts as good epistemic performance can be task- and situation-dependent and requires metacognitive judgment about when particular strategies are applicable
target_learners: learners engaged in online inquiry, model-based science, and belief formation across diverse tasks
target_learning_goals: forming accurate beliefs through reliable processes guided by metacognitive awareness of when and how skills can be used successfully
examples: Table 2 illustrates how successful, competent, apt, and fully apt performance apply to forming beliefs, judging online claim accuracy, and model-based inquiry in science

article_title: The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning
citation: Richard E. Mayer. (2024). The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09842-1
title: SOI model: selecting, organizing, and integrating as the core cognitive processes of CTML
description: The SOI model holds that meaningful learning depends on three cognitive processes: selecting relevant material for further processing, organizing it into a coherent cognitive representation, and integrating it with relevant prior knowledge. The article states that "The SOI model was a major conceptual breakthrough for me, and has remained at the core of CTML ever since". In the current model CTML has five cognitive processes: selecting words, selecting images, organizing words, organizing images, and integrating.
requirements: Learners must engage in appropriate cognitive processing during learning for meaningful learning to occur
target_learners: students learning from multimedia instructional messages
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning of academic material
examples: Instructional design is intended to guide these processes, such as prompting learners to write a summary or self-test during pauses in a lesson.

article_title: Introducing the FoRe-Squares Model: Focus Support and Reward as Key Predictors of Effective Technology-Augmented Instruction
citation: Eitel, A., Krebs, M.-C., Schöne, C. (2025). Introducing the FoRe-Squares Model: Focus Support and Reward as Key Predictors of Effective Technology-Augmented Instruction. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10045-z
title: Active goal-directed processing as the SOISG mediator of learning outcomes
description: The model's mediating variable, active goal-directed processing, consists of five cognitive processes abbreviated SOISG: selecting, organizing, and integrating (SOI, per cognitive theory of multimedia learning), strengthening (S, via rehearsal and retrieval), and generating (G, inferences mapping to similar and novel situations). The article notes "the more an instruction stimulates SOISG processing (selecting-organizing-integrating-strengthening-generating) in an active and goal-directed manner, the more likely the instruction is to foster learning outcomes." Strengthening is described as especially important for fluent recall, while generating is especially important for transfer. The construct is not directly observable but is indicated by behavioral data such as eye movements, think-aloud protocols, and key presses, enriched with physiological and questionnaire data.
requirements: Measurement via behavioral data best enriched with physiological data such as pupil dilation or EEG, plus questionnaire data on mental effort and mind wandering
constraints: Active goal-directed processing is not directly observable from the outside
target_learning_goals: recall and transfer of instructionally relevant content

article_title: The Role of School in Adolescents’ Identity Development. A Literature Review
citation: Verhoeven, M., Poorthuis, A. M. G., & Volman, M. (2019). The Role of School in Adolescents' Identity Development. A Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9457-3
title: Sociocultural perspective: identity as multidimensional self-understandings developed through participation in sociocultural contexts
description: The review describes the sociocultural perspective, under which identity is understood as "a multidimensional phenomenon rather than a single entity": people develop a range of self-understandings (e.g., science identity, literacy identity) that are integrated into learner, student, social, and personal identities. Identity develops through participation in contexts such as home, school, and work, where interaction makes identity positions available and tools, norms, and values guide action. Half of the reviewed articles (n = 55) employed this perspective.
requirements: Studies adopting this perspective examine how identity positions and their evaluation, and how tools, norms, and values communicated through educational activities, inform adolescents' identities
constraints: The review reports this perspective as used by the included studies, not as a tested result

citation: Luciano Gasser · Yvonne Dammert · P. Karen Murphy. (2022). How Do Children Socially Learn from Narrative Fiction: Getting the Lesson, Simulating Social Worlds, or Dialogic Inquiry? Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1445–1475. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09667-4
title: Sociomoral competence defined through theory of mind, empathy, and social reasoning
description: The review defines sociomoral competence as the ability to take the perspective of and feel emotional concern for another person as well as engage in complex social reasoning that aims to balance conflicting interests. It builds on three developmental concepts: ToM (understanding mental states), empathy (an affective response stemming from apprehension of another's emotional state), and social reasoning, which the authors consider more complex than ToM and empathy because it requires coordinating moral, social-conventional, and personal concerns in context-specific ways.

constraints: Social reasoning requiring coordination of multiple concerns represents a more complex sociomoral competence than ToM and empathy, which contribute to basic social functioning

examples: The review describes Social Domain Theory findings that preschoolers judge straightforward moral transgressions as wrong independently of authority, rules, and context

citation: Kopatz, M., Wagner, W., Neuendorf, C., Trautwein, U., Nagengast, B., and Bardach, L. (2025). description: The article draws on social contagion theory to explain motivational composition effects: "Social contagion describes the transmission of psychological characteristics (e.g., attitudes, behaviors, motivation) among individuals in a network (Levy & Nail, 1993)." article_title: Social contagion and high school dropout: The role of friends, romantic partners, and siblings.
citation: Dupéré, V., Dion, E., Cantin, S., Archambault, I., & Lacourse, E. (2021). Social contagion and high school dropout: The role of friends, romantic partners, and siblings. Journal of Educational Psychology, 113, 572-584. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000484
title: Social contagion of dropout through recent exposure within networks of same-age intimates
description: Social contagion refers to "the transmission of behaviors through contact with others who exhibit these behaviors". Applied to dropout, the article argues contagion is unlikely to occur through imitation of high-status models, since dropping out is uncorrelated or negatively correlated with peer-group status; it may instead operate through transmission of educational norms in communities where dropout is prevalent. Contagion is theorized to depend on recency of exposure, with dropout contagious only for a short period, and to be especially likely when adolescents with pre-existing vulnerabilities are in contact.
requirements: Contact between adolescents and same-age intimates who have recently exhibited the behavior
constraints: Only experimental or detailed longitudinal evidence with proper statistical controls can fully disentangle social influences from homophily and similarity-based selection
The mechanisms underlying contagion were not assessed in the present study

target_learning_goals: Understanding and preventing the social propagation of high school dropout

citation: van de Werfhorst, H. G., Zwier, D., Geven, S., Bol, T. & Haelermans, C. (2024). Inequality in pandemic effects on school track placement and the role of social and academic embeddedness. npj Science of Learning 9:71. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00283-1

description: The article applies a sociological embeddedness framework in which "social integration in intermediary organizations and networks fosters compliance with dominant norms, provides information, and enables the sharing of resources." Embeddedness is of two kinds: social (parents integrated in school parental networks) and academic (motivation, self-efficacy, grit as embodied pro-school orientations). The framework predicts these resources matter especially when schooling is disrupted and students rely more on themselves and their parents.

article_title: Commensality and academic performance: measuring peer acceptance among college students
citation: Jinxi Wen, Wenjing Lyu, Jin Liu & Li Yang. (2025). Commensality and academic performance: measuring peer acceptance among college students. npj Science of Learning 10:69. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00357-8
title: Social capital account: commensality as a behavioral proxy for peer acceptance that grants bonding and bridging social capital
description: The article interprets its findings through social capital theory, proposing that "commensality serves as a behavioral proxy for peer acceptance, a social state that, in turn, grants students access to valuable social capital." Roommate commensality is aligned with bonding social capital offering emotional support through strong, trust-based ties, while commensality with more distant peers reflects bridging social capital that grants access to diverse information and perspectives. The framework is used to explain why the most physically distant peers showed the strongest associations.
requirements: Requires measurement of shared-meal behavior (commensality value) as the behavioral proxy for peer acceptance
constraints: The authors state the direction of causality cannot be determined from their data, so the account is interpretive rather than causally tested
target_learners: first-year undergraduate students in high-residential universities
target_learning_goals: academic performance (semester average scores, major ranking, failed subjects)
examples: The article proposes that interactions with more distant peers are intentional choices that bridge structural holes in the university's social network, sources of unique information and diverse perspectives

article_title: Body-part specificity for learning of multiple prior distributions in human coincidence timing
citation: Yoshiki Matsumura, Neil W. Roach, James Heron & Makoto Miyazaki. (2024). Body-part specificity for learning of multiple prior distributions in human coincidence timing. npj Science of Learning 9:34. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00241-x
title: Somatotopic organisation hypothesis for body-part specific learning of multiple priors
description: The article proposes that body-part specific learning of temporal priors is organised somatotopically, drawing on the supplementary motor area (SMA), which shows both time-interval tuning, action selectivity, and somatotopic body-part mapping. The authors infer that "when the neural representations of the body parts in the SMA are identical and close, the assigned priorsare generalised. However, when those in the SMA are distant, the assigned priors are independently acquired." The cerebellum and basal ganglia, which also show somatotopy and timing-related activity, are offered as complementary possible neural bases.
requirements: Convergent neuroimaging or neurophysiological evidence to identify the actual neural bases
constraints: The neural-basis discussion is acknowledged by the authors as merely speculative; whether body-part specificity operates in nontemporal tasks remains unclear
target_learners: healthy adult participants performing sensorimotor timing tasks
target_learning_goals: concurrent learning of multiple statistical priors tied to different motor effectors
examples: Experiment 4 and 5 (hand vs foot) showed concurrent learning from the earliest trial bin, whereas adjacent-finger assignment required more trials

article_title: Social interaction shapes and boosts second language learning: virtual reality can show us how
citation: Ana Zappa, Mel Slater & Antoni Rodriguez-Fornells. (2025). Social interaction shapes and boosts second language learning: virtual reality can show us how. npj Science of Learning 10:90. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00381-8
title: Social L2 Learning (SL2) model: L2 learning in real-life or simulated social interaction, with context quality explaining L1–L2 differences
description: The Social L2 Learning (SL2) model, proposed by Li and Jeong, defines socially interactive L2 learning as "real-life or simulated real-life environments where learners can interact with objects and people, perform actions, receive, use, and integrate perceptual, visuospatial, and other sensorimotor information". It claims L2 learning processes differ from L1 acquisition mainly because L2 learning contexts are generally poorer, and grounds its premises in memory research, including the encoding-specificity principle: retrieval is facilitated when learners are in the context in which they first encoded the material. The review uses the model to interpret neural evidence that social encoding yields more native-like processing.
requirements: Learning environments must allow interaction with objects and people and integration of perceptual, visuospatial, and sensorimotor information so that learning and communication become embodied.
constraints: The article notes the model cannot convincingly be tested via flat-screen paradigms such as video viewing or imagined social partners that bear little resemblance to naturalistic L1 acquisition.
target_learning_goals: Second language proficiency achieved through socially embedded communication
examples: The review cites fMRI studies of social vs. translation word encoding and live vs. video sign-syntax learning as supporting the model's prediction that richer social contexts yield more native-like processing.

citation: Ping Li and Hyeonjeong Jeong. (2020). The social brain of language: grounding second language learning in social interaction. npj Science of Learning 5:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0068-7
title: Social L2 Learning (SL2) framework: grounding adult L2 learning in real-life or simulated social interaction
description: The SL2 framework argues that adult second-language learning should be grounded in social interaction, defined as "learning through real-life or simulated real-life environments where learners can interact with objects and people, perform actions, receive, use, and integrate perceptual, visuospatial, and other sensorimotor information". It draws on the New Science of Learning, the Competition Model, encoding-specificity, and embodied cognition theories, and combines neurocognitive bases with social cognition. The article presents SL2 both as a theoretical hypothesis and a practical model for technology-based learning.
requirements: Learning contexts must permit interaction with objects and people and integration of perceptual, visuospatial, and sensorimotor information so that learning becomes embodied
constraints: The proposed SL2 brain network hypothesis of dynamic connection to the theory-of-mind network "needs to be examined carefully by comparing learning with social interaction versus without"

native-like lexico-semantic representation
communicative competence

article_title: Examining Student Teachers’ Agency in an AI-Supported Learning Environment: Q Methodology Research
citation: Chaaban, Y., Jung, S.-G., Medina, J., Azem, J. Y., Salminen, J., & Jansen, B. J. (2025). Examining Student Teachers' Agency in an AI-Supported Learning Environment: Q Methodology Research. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00529-y
title: Socio-cognitive three-dimension framework of student agency in AI-supported learning environments
description: The study draws on Bandura's socio-cognitive perspective, which views agency as a dynamic interplay between personal capacities and environmental resources rather than purely individual or socially determined. The authors state: "we draw on socio-cognitive perspectives in exploring the perceptions of student agency within AI-supported learning environments along three dimensions: intrapersonal, behavioral and environmental." The intrapersonal dimension covers beliefs, self-efficacy, motivation, interest, attitude and knowledge; the behavioral dimension covers self-directed learning including goal setting, monitoring, self-reflection and ethical evaluation; the environmental dimension covers learning atmosphere, interdependence, student-instructor relations, resources, criticality and authorship. The Q sample of 37 statements was categorized across these three dimensions.
requirements: Q sample statements categorized across the three dimensions based on the literature-based conceptualization
constraints: The framework was adapted from existing literature on student agency in a university context and served as a departure point for this study
target_learning_goals: Understanding and enacting student agency while using GenAI systems for academic work
examples: The 37-statement Q sample was split into 13 intrapersonal, 11 behavioral and 13 environmental statements

article_title: Evaluating a Persuasive Intervention for Engagement in a Large University Class
citation: Orji, F. A., Greer, J., & Vassileva, J. (2021). Evaluating a Persuasive Intervention for Engagement in a Large University Class. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00260-4
title: Socially-oriented persuasive strategies implemented as social visualizations of student performance data in a learning support system.
description: This design pattern implements persuasive strategies (social learning, social comparison, competition) as social visualizations showing students' assessment grades inside a learning support system. The article states "The persuasive strategy defines what information is visualized, e.g. whether the student can see just the score of the group (social learning) or also their own score to easily compare it with that of the group (social comparison) and or with specific peers (competition)." The visualizations update dynamically and include emoji feedback, and the authors note they "use familiar designs and can be implemented in any domain to represent various measures of student performance."
requirements: Access to student assessment grade data to populate the visualizations
Pseudonymized display of peers' grades and points to protect privacy while letting each viewer see their own real ID
A learning support system into which the visualizations can be integrated
constraints: The article notes it was not possible to make the behaviour of others directly observable due to the asynchronous nature of the online activities and privacy considerations, so the social learning strategy was implemented as aggregated performance of other students
target_learners: University students in large blended undergraduate courses
target_learning_goals: Increased engagement in online learning activities
examples: The article implemented three versions: a social comparison visualization showing the class average and the grades of five random higher-performing students, a social learning visualization showing grade ranges and the number of students within each range, and a competition visualization awarding points and ranking students on a leaderboard.

citation: Orji, F. A., Greer, J., & Vassileva, J. (2021). Evaluating a Persuasive Intervention for Engagement in a Large University Class. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00260-4
title: Socially-oriented persuasive strategies: social learning, upward social comparison, and competition.
description: The article defines "socially-oriented strategies" as "a class of persuasive strategies that provoke an intentional or unintentional change in an individual attitude or behaviour due to the influence of other people," drawing on social influence theory and Social Learning Theory. The three examined strategies are upward social comparison, in which people "compare themselves to similar others who are performing well"; social learning, where "the user learns through observation, imitation, and modelling the behaviour of others"; and competition, typically implemented as a leaderboard where users "can see their position relative to that of their peers." These strategies come from the Persuasive Systems Design Model's "social support" category of seven strategies.
requirements: A mechanism for informing users of the actions or performance of other users, such as social visualization, so that users can compare with, align with, or compete with others
constraints: The article notes these three strategies are commonly used in persuasive technology and have been shown successful at encouraging users in performing specific tasks, which is why they were chosen
target_learners: Students in blended and online higher-education courses
target_learning_goals: Motivating students to engage actively in learning activities

International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 31:24–56. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00228-w
title: Transition taxonomy: pragmatic and pedagogical social transitions organized by activity impact, group-size direction, and fluidity
description: The article presents a transition taxonomy that outlines the range of social transitions occurring in classrooms, distilled from prior literature and printed as Table 1. The taxonomy structured the scenarios used in both studies.

examples: Table 1 maps each of the 14 transition types to the Study 1 and Study 2 scenarios that elicited them, e.g. absence, late arrival, early dismissal, rotating activities, and within-activity group-size changes

anticipating unintended social effects of AI deployment in education

description: The article adapts a portion of social cognitive career theory (Lent et al., 1994) into a new model extending the Intrapersonal Technology Integration Scale by adding the four sources of self-efficacy (mastery experiences, vicarious information, verbal persuasion, emotional arousal) upstream of self-efficacy, outcome expectations, interests, and intentions. self-efficacy for educational technology

citation: Twining, P., Butler, D., Fisser, P., Leahy, M., Shelton, C., Forget-Dubois, N., & Lacasse, M. (2021). Developing a quality curriculum in a technological era. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 2285–2308. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09857-3
title: A sociocultural framework of educational alignment spanning national, local school and classroom levels
description: The article introduces a sociocultural framework for understanding curriculum change. As the abstract states, it "introduces a sociocultural framework that highlights the complexity of achieving alignment between policies and practice spanning the national to local school to classroom levels." The framework treats alignment as a multi-level problem: policies set at national level must be realised in local schools and ultimately in classrooms, and misalignment across these levels explains why curriculum reforms fail. constraints: The framework is presented as highlighting complexity rather than prescribing a single implementation mechanism

examples: The paper uses the framework to organise its expert-based exploration of stakeholder engagement, teacher professionalism and summative assessment

citation: Audio-Visual Communication Review. (1953). Audio-Visual Communication Review, 158. https://eric.ed.gov/
title: Social situation of contact as a factor in audience response to mass media
description: The digest presents the construct of the social situation of contact, defined as "the immediate social setting of contact with content and medium; that is, the people who are immediately involved in the individual's interactions when he is a member of the audience." Three basic situations were investigated: the child socially alone, the peer situation with friends, and the family situation with parents, grandparents, and much younger or older siblings. The study uses this construct to argue that audience response is shaped by the social setting of contact, not only by demographic attributes.

constraints: Evidence came from a limited audience that is not representative of the general population

target_learning_goals: understanding how the social setting of media contact shapes audience response
examples: The study interviewed 79 boys across kindergarten, second, fourth, and sixth grades about television, movies, and comic books

citation: Cirkony, C., Tytler, R., & Hubber, P. (2022). Designing and delivering representation-focused science lessons in a digital learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10094-z
title: Socio-semiotic theory underpinning the Representation Construction Approach
description: The article grounds RCA in socio-semiotics, in which meaning is made with signs within social and cultural contexts and is distributed across representational forms and modes. It states that "socio-semiotic theory considers meaning to be distributed across different representational forms (e.g., dialogue, written text, drawings, graphs, role-plays) and modes (i.e., verbal, written, visual, action) (Bezemer & Kress, 2016), each of which offers partial access to meaning." The study applies this perspective analytically to assess how the STILE platform facilitated students' meaning-making through generating and coordinating digital and non-digital multimodal representations.

constraints: No single representation can fully convey conceptual meaning, and there is no ideal representation

target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of science ideas such as energy transfer and the particle model
Representational competence and disciplinary literacy in science
examples: The study analysed Grade 9 students' drawings, role-plays, written responses, and annotated diagrams through a socio-semiotic lens across two STILE modules on heat transfer

title: Social practices of mutual understanding in asynchronous online discussion
description: A recurring set of six social practices that students used in asynchronous discussion boards to develop mutual understanding towards shared goals: invitation, provocation, identifying a common interest, reaching out, defending, and encouragement. The most common was identifying common interests (29 instances), followed by provocation (18). The authors note "The most commonly applied strategy was to seek to identify common interests", with students drawing out each other's interests through mutual self-disclosure or selectivity in the postings to which one responds.

article_title: Exploring learning in classic African board games: a review of recent literature
citation: Rebecca Y. Bayeck. (2026). Exploring learning in classic African board games: a review of recent literature. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10733-9
title: Sociocultural learning theory as the framework for understanding learning in classic African board games
description: The review draws on sociocultural learning theory (Vygotsky) to interpret learning in classic African board games. The theory holds that "humans are not isolated entities shaped by the context, but part of a social and cultural context they cannot be separated from". From this perspective, engagement and participation in activity and practice implies learning, so learning is always occurring and is not restricted to structured teaching. The review uses this lens to treat gameplay interactions, tool mediation, and problem solving with games as learning, framing classic African board games as analog technologies that mediate learning.
requirements: Learning is analyzed through participation in activities such as gameplay and through tools, artifacts, or others used to address local problems
constraints: The framework treats learning as socially mediated and culturally embedded, so it interprets learning broadly rather than measuring instructional outcomes
target_learners: players of classic African board games across class, age, and gender, including adult Songo players and school children in African communities
target_learning_goals: mathematics
computational thinking
literacies
cultural knowledge
AI understanding
examples: The review interprets Songo gameplay literacies (Bayeck 2019) and AI agent development for Ayo, Awale, and Ntxuva as instances of learning mediated by these games

Education Tech Research Dev (2012) 60:193-221. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-011-9217-2
title: SOLO-based coding scheme for quality of knowledge construction
description: Knowledge construction quality was operationalized with a content analysis coding scheme based on Veldhuis-Diermanse (2002), itself grounded in the SOLO taxonomy of Biggs and Collis. 'The original coding scheme consists of ﬁve hierarchical levels (after Biggs and Collis 1982; Biggs 1999) from basic to advanced': E prestructural, D unistructural, C multistructural, B relational, and A extended abstract. Contributions in the Drewlite comment screens were segmented into meaningful units, coded with level-specific verbs, scored 1-5 points, and averaged per student. Inter-rater Cohen's kappa was 0.78 for test 1 and 0.81 for test 2, with 85% identical scores on intra-coder retest.

constraints: Scores of three inactive students were excluded due to limited contributions, leaving 84 students in the analysis

article_title: Team design communication patterns in e-learning design and development
citation: Rapanta, C., Maina, M., Lotz, N., & Bacchelli, A. (2013). Team design communication patterns in e-learning design and development. Educational Technology Research and Development, 61(4), 581-605. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-013-9306-5
title: Team e-learning design as a socio-cognitive activity analyzed at micro, meso, and macro levels
description: The article frames team design as a socio-cognitive activity rooted in Bucciarelli (1984), in which any design task effort must be made explicit as a communication message and any communication task must relate to the design task. It operationalizes this with a three-level interaction analysis coding scheme: "(a) The micro level, which refers to how each person behaves as part of the team; (b) the meso level, which refers to emerging structures as behaviors of two or more participants; and (c) the macro level, which refers to the shared subject focus of the team." Design objects, moves, and sequences are coded in parallel with communication moves and sequences.

constraints: A main difficulty is the identification and separation of the cognitive from the social aspects of discourse in highly interdisciplinary teams

citation: Ana Cebollero-Salinas, Jacobo Cano-Escoriaza, Santos Orejudo. (2022). Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2022.104464
title: Socio-emotional e-competencies model: five sub-competencies specific to online interaction
description: The article adopts a model of "socio-emotional e-competencies", competencies developed specifically for online interaction rather than transferred from face-to-face contexts. It comprises five sub-competencies: emotional e-awareness ("the capacity to identify and understand one's own emotions in a virtual context"), emotional e-regulation, e-self-control of impulsiveness, emotional e-independence, and social e-competency. The model is grounded in the argument that virtual environments differ from face-to-face ones in pace, anonymity, and disinhibition, so online emotion perception and expression need differentiated evaluation. In this study the five sub-competencies, measured with the e-COM questionnaire (25 items, five subscales), serve as exogenous predictors of the habitual digital behaviors factor in a structural equation model.
requirements: Measurement requires the e-COM questionnaire or an equivalent instrument assessing the five sub-competencies in online settings
constraints: The article argues competencies evaluated outside the online environment cannot simply be treated as equivalent to online socio-emotional competencies, since virtual encounters occur under a different spatio-temporal set of circumstances

examples: The e-COM questionnaire operationalises the model with 25 items on an 11-point Likert scale, e.g., 'Before making a joke about someone on social media, I am capable of imagining how they are going to feel' for emotional e-regulation

article_title: Mood-affect congruency. Exploring the relation between learners’ mood and the affective charge of educational videos
citation: Maik Beege. (2019). Parasocial Learning – The Impacts of Social Entities in Learning with Educational Videos. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.05.001
title: Social Agency Theory and the CASA Paradigm explain why social cues in multimedia trigger social responses
description: The thesis describes social agency theory (Mayer, Sobko, & Mautone, 2003) and the Computers-Are-Social-Actors (CASA) paradigm as the framework explaining how social cues in multimedia learning trigger social responses. "Social cues in a multimedia environment (e.g., eye contact, voice, gestures) prime a social activation schema, which triggers processes of human-to-human communication." The CASA paradigm holds that "Social responses to computers are commonplace, unavoidable, and easy to generate." This framework underpins the thesis's expectation that design features of social entities in instructional videos influence learning.
requirements: A multimedia environment must contain social cues such as eye contact, voice, or gestures to prime a social activation schema
target_learning_goals: deep cognitive processing of multimedia learning material

title: Design social entities so benefits of social cues outweigh added cognitive costs
description: The thesis derives a design principle from the tension between cognitive load and social agency perspectives: "Social entities need to be integrated in such a way that the benefits at least outweigh the costs." Because "designing an instructor, filming instructional videos or programming, and designing pedagogical agents increase production cost, design recommendations should be specified." The principle calls for deliberate integration of social entities rather than blanket inclusion or exclusion.
requirements: Social entities must be integrated deliberately so that benefits of social cues at least outweigh the added processing costs
constraints: Studies report negative effects, positive effects, and zero effects of social cues on learning, so effects are moderated by entity appearance, voice, gesture, recipient characteristics, learning disciplines, and pacing
target_learners: designers of instructional videos and multimedia learning environments
target_learning_goals: optimizing learning processes with social entities in video-based instruction
examples: Study 1 manipulated addressing and proximity of a lecturer; study 2 manipulated agent age and primed text age; study 3 manipulated learner mood and video affective charge.

citation: Christopher T. Stripling and T. Grady Roberts. (2013). Effects of Mathematics Integration in a Teaching Methods Course on Self-Efficacy of Preservice Agricultural Education Teachers. Journal of Agricultural Education, 54(2), 114-129. https://doi.org/10.5032/jae.2013.02114
title: Bandura's social cognitive theory and its self-efficacy component as a framework for teacher efficacy development
description: The study is framed by Bandura's social cognitive theory, in which "a reciprocal relationship exists between personal factors, environmental factors, and behavior." constraints: The article notes that once teaching efficacy beliefs stabilize, they are difficult to change.
target_learning_goals: teaching contextualized mathematics
teacher efficacy development
examples: The study measured three efficacy constructs before, during, and after a mathematics integration treatment in a teaching methods course, testing whether a mastery-style experience (teaching math-enhanced lessons) changed efficacy beliefs.

target_learning_goals: English proficiency across phonological, lexico-grammatical and cultural dimensions

citation: Portolese Dias, L., & Trumpy, R. (2013). Online Instructor's Use of Audio Feedback to Increase Social Presence and Student Satisfaction.

citation: Hassan Alrayah. (2018). The Effectiveness of Cooperative Learning Activities in Enhancing EFL Learners' Fluency. English Language Teaching, 11(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n4p21

The article uses it to explain why cooperative efforts promote greater achievement and psychological health than competitive or individualistic efforts.

title: Social norms framework for contextual influences on achievement goals: classroom goal structures as injunctive norms and peer achievement goals as descriptive norms
description: The article integrates two previously isolated strands of research on contextual influences on individual achievement goals into a single social norms framework. Drawing on Cialdini's distinction that "Descriptive norms refer to what is typically done by most people in a setting and reflect the prevalence of a behaviour" while "Injunctive norms refer to what others consider acceptable or approve of," the framework conceptualizes class-level classroom goal structures as injunctive norms (messages about which goals are salient and accepted, conveyed through instructional practices) and peer achievement goals as descriptive norms (what classmates typically strive for). It proposes both influence individual achievement goals, depicted in a conceptual model (Figure 1), and is tested with longitudinal multilevel data from the transition to secondary school, a period when norms are especially powerful.

Classroom-level aggregation of student ratings so the shared context is empirically represented
constraints: Tested in German academic secondary schools (Gymnasium) mathematics classes within an individualistic Western culture
The role of injunctive norms needs further investigation; the authors refrain from conclusions about their general role

target_learning_goals: Individual achievement goals (mastery, performance-approach, performance-avoidance) in academic subject learning
examples: The framework was tested with multilevel models predicting changes in mastery, performance-approach, and performance-avoidance goals from class-level classroom goal structures and peer achievement goals

article_title: Team-based learning (TBL) curriculum combined with video vignettes improves performance of undergraduate medical students on OSCE compared with TBL alone.
citation: Feigerlova Eva, Ioan Iulia, Pape Elise, Boursier Caroline, Berguer Marion, Hani Hind, Braun Marc. (2024). Team-based learning (TBL) curriculum combined with video vignettes improves performance of undergraduate medical students on OSCE compared with TBL alone. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05861-w
title: Social learning theory as the design rationale for the TBL video-vignette curriculum
description: The authors ground the module's construction in social learning theory, stating that "1) observed behavior must be noteworthy to get the attention of students and to be memorized; 2) behavior should be facile to reproduce; and 3) the subject must motivate students." Video vignettes of exemplary clinical situations serve as the observed behavior, and team-based collaborative activities with peers and tutors supply the environmental factors the theory emphasizes. The authors also draw on Croskerry's distinction between rapid pattern-recognition thinking and slow mechanistic thinking to justify building repertoires of exemplary situations.
requirements: Video vignettes must portray noteworthy, reproducible behavior that motivates students, and the module must retain collaborative activities with peers and tutors
constraints: The authors present this as the design rationale supporting their strategy, not as a tested mechanism; they offer candidate explanations (contextual linkage of vignettes, less interaction in the written-script setting, easier transfer of video patterns to clinical settings) without testing them
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning and pattern recognition for rare conditions
self-reflection and critical thinking through exemplary clinical situations
examples: Instructors presented illness scripts successively as teams progressed through a complex patient case, with video vignettes watched on a central screen in the presence of instructors

article_title: Impact of flipped classroom model in increasing the achievement for medical students.
citation: Sourg Hanadi Abdelgadir Ahmed, Satti Shahenaz, Ahmed Nasereldin, Ahmed Adil Ballal Mohammed. (2023). Impact of flipped classroom model in increasing the achievement for medical students. BMC Medical Education, 23, 287. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04276-3
title: Socrative-supported iRAT and tRAT sequence in the flipped classroom session
description: The flipped classroom session used an individual readiness assurance test (iRAT) followed by a team readiness assurance test (tRAT), then PowerPoint-based discussion, concept recall writing, and peer question exchange. The online platform Socrative hosted the tests: "The iRAT and tRAT were conductued in Socrative which is an on line application in which you can conduct quizzes, surveys, team activities, and educational content". Students received individual scores without knowing which questions were correct, then debated issues and taught concepts to one another in teams.
requirements: Students must access pre-class learning materials (objectives, reading materials, a five-minute video, and 20-minute summary slides) uploaded to the application prior to the scheduled session
target_learning_goals: concept recall of lecture content
in-class application and collaborative discussion
examples: Group A received topic-specific objectives, learning materials, a five-minute video and 20-minute summary slides two days before class, then completed iRAT, tRAT, discussion and application exercises in class

article_title: The quality of group interactions in medical problem-based learning in China: the roles of intercultural sensitivity and group ethnic composition.
citation: Wang Rong, Liu Chuanyong, Zhang Shu-Yong. (2023). The quality of group interactions in medical problem–based learning in China: the roles of intercultural sensitivity and group ethnic composition. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04616-3
title: Sociocultural Theory as the conceptual basis linking cultural diversity to group interaction processes
description: The article adopts Sociocultural Theory, together with the sociocultural perspective of collaborative learning, to explain why cultural diversity affects the quality of PBL group interaction. It holds that "The Sociocultural Theory posits that culture make an impact on students' learning behavior (e.g., group interactions)", so a student who understands and appreciates cultural differences and maintains positive emotion is more likely to succeed in group learning. Intercultural sensitivity is positioned as the individual-level factor moderating diversity's effect on interaction processes.
requirements: Measurable individual differences in intercultural sensitivity (here the Chen and Starosta ISS) and identified interaction dimensions (exploratory questions, cumulative reasoning, handling conflict) to operationalize the theory in PBL
constraints: Applied here to medical PBL in a Chinese university setting with Chinese and international students
target_learners: Medical undergraduates learning in culturally heterogeneous small groups
target_learning_goals: Collaborative learning behavior and interaction quality in small-group problem-based learning
examples: The authors used the theory to select intercultural sensitivity, ethnic composition and personal characteristics as predictors in their regression models of the three interaction types

article_title: Evaluation of a digital game for teaching behavioral aspects of clinical communication in dentistry.
citation: Lin Chia-Shu, Yang Cheng-Chieh. (2023). Evaluation of a digital game for teaching behavioral aspects of clinical communication in dentistry. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04040-7
title: Social Cognitive Theory account of game-induced self-efficacy gains
description: The authors interpret the self-efficacy increases using Social Cognitive Theory: "such an increased self-efficacy may reflect higher expectancies of the outcome of clinical communication." Experiencing game scenes about managing older patients makes students aware that understanding patients' physical conditions is critical, which they link to students' self-efficacy ratings. The theory frames the game as providing vicarious mastery-like experience of clinical contexts.
requirements: Learners must lack prior clinical experience for the vicarious context to add new self-efficacy
constraints: The authors present this as an interpretation, not a tested mechanism
target_learning_goals: self-efficacy in clinical communication skills
examples: After playing scenes #1, #6, and #14 about older patients, students became aware that understanding patients' physical conditions is critical

article_title: Resuscitation simulation among people who are likely to witness opioid overdose: Experiences from the SOONER Trial.
citation: Whittall Jonathan P., Orkin Aaron M., Handford Curtis, Klaiman Michelle, Leece Pamela, Charles Mercy, Wright Amy, Turner Suzanne, Morrison Laurie J., Strike Carol, Campbell Douglas M. (2022). Resuscitation simulation among people who are likely to witness opioid overdose: Experiences from the SOONER Trial. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0270829
title: SOONER high-fidelity opioid overdose simulation protocol
description: A three-component simulation protocol — standardized video briefing, a staged near-fatal overdose scenario using a Laerdal SimMan® ALS manikin in a staged bedroom, and a PEARLS-adapted debriefing — based on 2015 American Heart Association bystander resuscitation recommendations. Scenario design and testing was "done with community members who had lived experience with opioid overdose", and performance was video-recorded and scored by two clinicians blinded to allocation.
requirements: Successful resuscitation required participants to administer intranasal naloxone and perform chest compressions, with recognition, positioning, EMS activation and organization also evaluated
constraints: Designed to mimic a very near-fatal overdose; without prompt intervention the simulated patient would proceed to cardiac arrest and death
target_learners: Non-clinicians at high risk of experiencing or witnessing opioid overdose, aged over 16
target_learning_goals: Navigating the bystander resuscitation algorithm for opioid overdose
examples: A phone in the room allowed simulated 911 calls answered by research coordinators; the simulation lasted 5–10 minutes and ended with simulated EMS arrival

article_title: Effects of Gamification on the Benefits of Student Response Systems in Learning of Human Anatomy: Three Experimental Studies.
citation: López-Jiménez, J. J., Fernández-Alemán, J. L., García-Berná, J. A., López González, L., González Sequeros, O., Nicolás Ros, J., Carrillo de Gea, J. M., Idri, A., & Toval, A. (2021). Effects of Gamification on the Benefits of Student Response Systems in Learning of Human Anatomy: Three Experimental Studies. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph182413210
title: Social Comparison Theory explains the dual effect of leaderboards: competition motivates some students while discouraging lower-performing ones
description: The article invokes Social Comparison Theory (SCT), under which "each individual possesses an inherent drive to receive accurate self-evaluations". It uses SCT to explain why visible rankings helped the 57 of 90 students with predominantly positive ranking variations but harmed the 33 students with predominantly negative variations, who scored below the group mean (7.14 vs 7.44). Rankings are said to produce stress, feelings of inferiority and reduced autonomy and competence in lower performers.
requirements: Instructors must manage leaderboard visibility (e.g. showing rankings only at test end and clearing scores at the next test start) to limit harmful comparison.
constraints: The motivating effect of competition varies with ethnicity, society, age and individual learning-style preferences, per the article.
target_learners: first-year medical students in human anatomy
target_learning_goals: musculoskeletal anatomy knowledge
engagement and motivation in classroom quizzes
examples: The article reports 33 of 90 students in the badge cohort had more negative than positive ranking variations and scored 7.14 on the final exam versus a group mean of 7.44.
